After providing informed consent, participants completed a CBCA training, which included one of two practice statements.
After four multiple choice attention checks on the practice statements, participants were randomly assigned to the control, full-information, or sequencing condition.

table.title: Truth or Lie? Impact of Sequencing Case Information on Credibility Assessment
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
H1 Bias hypothesis: CBCA is prone to contextual bias.
H1a: The CBCA sum score of the full-information condition is lower than the CBCA sum score of the control condition, indicating that contextual bias affects CBCA sum scores.
H1b: The credibility judgement of the full-information condition is lower than the credibility judgement of the control condition, indicating that contextual bias affects credibility judgments.
H2 Debiasing hypothesis: Sequencing protects against contextual bias.
H2a: The CBCA sum score of the full information condition is lower than the CBCA sum score of the sequencing information condition.
H2b: The credibility judgement of the full-information condition is lower than the credibility judgement of the sequencing information condition.
Auxiliary hypothesis: We also aim to rule out pre-bias differences between the sequencing and control conditions. Therefore, we will test the null hypothesis that CBCA sum scores do not differ between these conditions before any biasing contextual information is presented.
table.design_dependent_variables:
1) CBCA sum score consisting of the summing of the scores of four pre-selected CBCA criteria (CBCA criteria 1, 3, 7 and 14; Steller & Köhnken, 1989). Each criterion is paraphrased, e.g. the statement must be rich in detail, including specific descriptions of place, time, persons, objects, and events, and rated on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).
2) Credibility judgment as a single item ( "Focusing just on her statement, how credible/believable do you rate Tina Schmidt's statement?") judged on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (not credible at all) to 7 (extremely credible).
table.study_design_overview:
Random assignment to one of three experimental conditions that differ in whether and at what stage contextual case information is presented:
• Control condition with no contextual case information
• Full information condition: contextual information before CBCA scoring
• Sequencing condition: contextual information after CBCA scoring (yet before the credibility judgment)
In addition, they will be assigned to one of two practice statements during the CBCA training, but this assignment is independent of the key conditions mentioned above.
table.statistical_tests:
H1:  We will conduct a Bayesian ANOVA with the sum CBCA score as the dependent variable and experimental condition (full-information vs. debiasing vs. control) as the independent variable. We will compare a model including a main effect of condition to a null model (i.e., at least one pairwise difference vs. no differences).
Planned contrasts. All main hypotheses are directional; therefore, all planned Bayesian t-tests for these contrasts will be one-tailed.
	H1a.  The dependent variable is the CBCA sum score, and the independent variable is the condition (full-information < control condition).
	H1b.  The dependent variable is the credibility judgment, and the independent variable is the condition (full-information < control condition).
H2.  We will conduct a Bayesian ANOVA with credibility judgment as the dependent variable and experimental condition (full-information vs. sequencing vs. control) as the independent variable. Again, we will compare a model including a main effect of condition to a null model.
Planned contrasts. All main hypotheses are directional; therefore, all planned Bayesian t-tests for these contrasts will be one-tailed.
	H2a.  The dependent variable is the CBCA sum score, and the independent variable is the condition (full-information < sequencing condition).
	H2b.  The dependent variable is the credibility judgment, and the independent variable is the condition (full-information < sequencing condition).
Auxiliary hypothesis: We will use a two-tailed t-test because we do not expect a systematic difference in either direction. The dependent variable is the CBCA sum score, and the independent variables are the conditions (we will compare only the sequencing and control conditions; sequencing = control condition).
table.outliers_and_exclusions: Data are excluded if the study was not completed, or the attention test was not passed. The attention tests consist of six questions in total (4 on the practice statement, one on case introduction, one on the victim statement, and one condition dependent on the contextual information). If participants fail one of the practice statement checks, and/or if they fail the victim statement or/and the condition-dependent check, they will be excluded.
table.sample_size:
Participants will be recruited online via Prolific (www.prolific.com).
The sample size will be determined using a Bayesian sequential design. However, the initial benchmark is based on a frequentist power analysis conducted with G*Power (α = .05 and power = .90) and indicates that at least 207 participants are required to detect a medium effect in an omnibus fixed-effects ANOVA (Arui et al., 2025). To account for potential exclusions, the first batch will include 240 participants. We will then proceed with a Bayesian sequential approach: by adding one more batch of 240 new participants, if the Bayes factor does not exceed 5. Data collection will continue iteratively until the Bayes factor in favor of either hypothesis (H1) exceeds 5. For feasibility reasons, data collection will be capped at a maximum of 480 participants, regardless of the Bayes factor.
table.additional_comments:
This is a replication/ extension study (https://osf.io/5hpfm/) with the key difference that we now add a more detailed CBCA training, including the specific criteria, and added a training statement with feedback that allows us to check whether the participants rate the CBCA criteria as instructed. To do this, first, participants will watch a short video explaining that they will use a method that assesses the truthfulness of a victim's statement based on content criteria. This is followed by four short clips, one for each criterion. In these videos, the meaning of each criterion is explained and then demonstrated with two examples: one in which the criterion has a high presence and one in which the presence is low, to illustrate how different statements may look. Subsequently, participants will be presented with a more extensive example (one of two counterbalanced practice statements), in which two of the criteria show high presence and two show low presence. 
•	Practice Statement 1: CBCA criteria 1 and 3 are strong, CBCA criteria 7 and 14 are weak
•	Practice Statement 2: CBCA criteria 1 and 3 are weak, CBCA criteria 7 and 14 are strong
They will then be asked to rate the statement on all four criteria. Afterwards, they will receive the expected ranking and an explanation and will answer four multiple-choice questions regarding the ranking of each criterion.
To check the Practice Statement performance, we run four one-tailed independent Bayesian t-tests comparing Practice Statement 1 and 2 (independent variable) on the score for each CBCA criterion (score on CBCA criteria 1, 3, 7 or 14 as dependent variable). We expect that participants who received Practice Statement 1 will score higher on criteria 1 and 3 than participants who received Practice Statement 2. In addition, we expect that participants with Practice Statement 2 will score criteria 7 and 14 higher than participants with Practice Statement 1.

live_data_statements: In a preregistered online experiment, 242 participants completed a CBCA training and made a credibility judgment of a victim statement based on their CBCA scoring.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions that varied in the timing of contextual information.
Participants were recruited via Prolific (www.prolific.com) and completed the study online through Qualtrics, in return for £8.63 per hour.

The size of the initial batch (n = 240) was based on a frequentist power analysis conducted with G*Power (α = .05 and power = .90) that indicates that at least 207 participants were required to detect a medium effect (Arui et al., 2025) in an omnibus fixed-effects ANOVA.

Participants were excluded if they failed one or more of the following attention checks: One out of the four practice-statement attention checks, the victim-statement attention check, or the condition-dependent attention check.
These participants were on average 34.2 years old (SD = 12.7).
Participants were recruited on Prolific for a study on determining whether a victim statement is true or false, which contained a trigger warning for child sexual abuse.
After providing informed consent, participants completed a CBCA training, which included one of two practice statements.
After four multiple choice attention checks on the practice statements, participants were randomly assigned to the control, full-information, or sequencing condition.

For the overall credibility judgment, all participants were instructed to focus on the victim's statement and reminded that the more criteria are present, the more truthful the statement is considered (see Materials) Afterwards, they were asked to rank the order in which the four CBCA criteria or other information had determined their credibility judgment.
Finally, participants were thanked, debriefed, and paid.

Subsequently, participants were presented with one of two counterbalanced practice statements, in which two of the criteria show high presence, and two show low presence (Practice Statement 1: CBCA criteria 1 and 3 are highly present, CBCA criteria 7 and 14 are weakly present; Practice Statement 2: CBCA criteria 1 and 3 are weakly present, CBCA criteria 7 and 14 are strongly present) Participants were then asked to rate the statement on all four criteria.

Participants had been randomly assigned to a practice statement that was designed to score high on 2 and low on 2 other CBCA criteria (i.e., practice statement1 scored high on Logical Structure and Quantity of Details and low on Spontaneous Corrections and Unexpected Complications; practice statement1 scored high on Spontaneous Corrections and Unexpected Complications and low on Logical Structure and Quantity of Details).
These results indicate that participants were able to apply the criteria as intended for either practice statement.
In this study, participants were not explicitly instructed to refrain from using background information in their credibility judgments.

info.title: Sequencing as a Debiasing Strategy for Credibility Assessment: Protection for CBCA Scoring but Not Final Credibility Judgments

author.affiliation: Max Planck Institute for the Study of Crime, Security, and Law

text.text: Criteria-Based Content Analysis (CBCA) is used to assess the credibility of victim statements, e.g., in child sexual abuse cases.
Prior work showed that contextual case information can bias both CBCA scores and the resulting credibility judgments.
We examined whether sequencing case information can prevent such contextual bias.
Prior research could not fully test the effectiveness of sequencing as a debiasing strategy as the bias induction was unsuccessful.
This inspired this new, improved study design.
In a preregistered online experiment, 242 participants completed a CBCA training and made a credibility judgment of a victim statement based on their CBCA scoring.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions that varied in the timing of contextual information.
In the control condition, participants received no biasing contextual information.
In the full-information condition, credibility-reducing contextual biasing information was presented before the victim statement.
In the sequencing condition, biasing contextual information was presented after the CBCA rating.
Bayesian analyses showed that both CBCA scores and credibility judgments were lower in the fullinformation condition than in the control condition, indicating contextual bias.
Sequencing prevented bias in CBCA scores: CBCA ratings in the sequencing condition were higher than in the full-information condition and comparable to the control condition.
However, sequencing did not prevent contextual bias in subsequent credibility judgments.

These findings indicate that sequencing can help protect CBCA from contextual influences, but additional safeguards are needed to prevent irrelevant background case information from shaping final credibility judgments.

Recent public debates about sexual abuse, most notably the #MeToo movement and widely publicized cases (Hörnle, 2021), show how central, contested, and consequential credibility judgments of alleged victims have become.

(2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Von Oppen et al., 2026</ref>; CBCA: d = 0.33; final credibility judgments: d = 0.88).

text.text: These findings suggest that CBCA criteria are susceptible to contextual influences, at least under certain circumstances.
How can we safeguard CBCA-based assessments against contextual bias?
While there have been several proposals (Neal & Brodsky, 2016; Vredeveldt et al., 2024), forensic psychology currently lacks evidence-based methods to successfully mitigate bias.
text.formatted: While there have been several proposals <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Neal & Brodsky, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Vredeveldt et al., 2024)</ref>, forensic psychology currently lacks evidence-based methods to successfully mitigate bias.

text.text: At the same time, forensic science has not just studied but implemented debiasing methods in practice, including the sequencing of case information (Dror, 2020; Dror & Kukucka, 2021).
text.formatted: At the same time, forensic science has not just studied but implemented debiasing methods in practice, including the sequencing of case information <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Dror, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Dror & Kukucka, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: One prominent example is Linear Sequential Unmasking (LSU), where a case manager controls the order of information given to the forensic expert (Dror & Kukucka, 2021; Dror et al., 2015).
text.formatted: One prominent example is Linear Sequential Unmasking (LSU), where a case manager controls the order of information given to the forensic expert <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Dror & Kukucka, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Dror et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The core idea is that one cannot be biased by information one does not know of (yet).
Experts therefore first only receive the strictly necessary raw crime-scene evidence (e.g., the fingerprint, or the DNA sample) and only later any required contextual information.
Sequencing helps to ensure one works from the evidence to the suspect, not the other way around.

A challenge to translate the sequencing approach from the forensic sciences to legal and forensic psychology is to determine what is relevant versus irrelevant for the task at hand (Skeem et al., 1998; Gardner et al., 2019).
text.formatted: A challenge to translate the sequencing approach from the forensic sciences to legal and forensic psychology is to determine what is relevant versus irrelevant for the task at hand <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Skeem et al., 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Gardner et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: LSU-Expanded (LSU-E) adds the criteria of biasing power, objectivity, and relevance to guide the order in which information is revealed (Dror & Kukucka, 2021).
text.formatted: LSU-Expanded (LSU-E) adds the criteria of biasing power, objectivity, and relevance to guide the order in which information is revealed <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Dror & Kukucka, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: For fingerprint matching, the relevant material is the fingerprint, and all other information (e.g., the ethnic origin of the suspect, a strong alibi, or a DNA match) can be regarded as contextual.
Forensic psychologists, however, are likely to differ in opinion on what is relevant or irrelevant for credibility assessment (Neal et al., 2019; Oeberst & Oberlader, 2024).
text.formatted: Forensic psychologists, however, are likely to differ in opinion on what is relevant or irrelevant for credibility assessment <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Neal et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Oeberst & Oberlader, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: For example, is the opinion of another expert, a Rorschach test, a retracted confession, or the modus operandi in another crime relevant?
Moreover, in some countries, forensic-psychological experts who assess victim statements may obtain contextual information by interacting with the victim in an interview.
In sum, forensic psychology practice brings in aspects that inevitably introduce contextual information, and it can be difficult to distinguish task-relevant from irrelevant information.

At the same time, there seems promise in trying to translate the established practice of sequencing case information from the forensic sciences to credibility assessment: It may help to mitigate bias in parts of the procedure and make the influence of the contextual information transparent (Kukucka & Quigley-McBride, 2025; Oberlader & Verschuere, 2025).

text.text: To date, only one study has attempted to apply sequencing of case information as a debiasing method in credibility assessment using CBCA (Arui et al., 2025).
text.formatted: To date, only one study has attempted to apply sequencing of case information as a debiasing method in credibility assessment using CBCA <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Arui et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: They randomly assigned 467 participants to one of three conditions: control (no contextual information), fullinformation (contextual information along with the statement) or sequencing (first statement only, contextual information only after the CBCA scoring).
The contextual information concerned the opinion of a clinician that the alleged victim showed no signs of abuse.
Each participant received a brief introduction to the CBCA, scored the victim statement on four CBCA criteria, and came to a final credibility assessment.

Sequencing did not diminish contextual bias on the final credibility assessment, as participants who received the biasing information at any time point judged the statement as less credible than participants who received no contextual information.
Yet, the brief explanation of the CBCA criteria may not have been sufficient to assure adequate scoring of the criteria.
Moreover, findings regarding sequencing were inconclusive because there was no contextual bias in CBCA scores to begin with.
Consequently, the effectiveness of sequencing as a debiasing method for CBCA could not be fully evaluated.
We therefore re-assess the potential of sequencing to mitigate contextual bias in CBCA-based credibility assessment.
We aim to test whether sequencing can protect CBCA ratings from contextual bias by adapting the design of Arui et al. (2025) in two important ways.
text.formatted: We aim to test whether sequencing can protect CBCA ratings from contextual bias by adapting the design of <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Arui et al. (2025)</ref> in two important ways.

text.text: First, we used contextual information that was previously shown to induce bias (a combination of multiple elements reducing credibility including a previous false accusation by the victim and the victim displaying behavioral problems; Bogaard et al., 2014; Von Oppen et al., 2026).
text.formatted: First, we used contextual information that was previously shown to induce bias (a combination of multiple elements reducing credibility including a previous false accusation by the victim and the victim displaying behavioral problems; <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Bogaard et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Von Oppen et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Secondly, to ensure that participants understand and appropriately apply the CBCA criteria, we moved from a brief explanation to a more extensive CBCA training, including examples for each criterion, as well as feedback on CBCA scoring of each criterion.
Participants first received said CBCA training, then were randomly assigned to one of three conditions (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: Participants first received said CBCA training, then were randomly assigned to one of three conditions (see Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: In the control condition, participants did not receive any contextual biasing information during the experiment.
They listened to and read the victim statement, rated it on the CBCA criteria, and then provided a credibility judgment.

In the full-information condition, participants first received credibilityreducing contextual information, then listened to the statement, and subsequently rated the CBCA criteria and provided a credibility judgment.

In the debiasing condition, participants first listened to the statement and rated the CBCA criteria; only afterward would they receive the contextual information and then provide the credibility judgment.
We will test the following hypotheses: H1.

CBCA is prone to contextual bias: The CBCA score in the full-information condition will be lower than in the control condition, indicating that contextual bias affects CBCA scores (H1a); and the credibility judgment in the full-information condition will be lower than in the control condition, indicating that contextual bias affects credibility judgments (H1b).

Sequencing protects against contextual bias: The CBCA score in the full-information condition will be lower than in the sequencing condition (H2a); the credibility judgment in the full-information condition will be lower than in the sequencing condition (H2b).

text.text: Participants were recruited on Prolific for a study on determining whether a victim statement is true or false, which contained a trigger warning for child sexual abuse.
After providing informed consent, participants completed a CBCA training, which included one of two practice statements.
After four multiple choice attention checks on the practice statements, participants were randomly assigned to the control, full-information, or sequencing condition.
Participants in the full information condition first received the contextual biasing information, followed by the victim statement.
They then scored the four CBCA criteria and provided an overall credibility judgment.

Participants in the sequencing condition first listened to the victim statement and scored the CBCA criteria, then received the contextual biasing information and provided an overall credibility judgment.
Participants in the control condition only received the victim statement, then scored the CBCA criteria and provided an overall credibility judgment (see Figure 1).

text.text: CBCA training.
First, participants watched a short video (1:00 minute) explaining that they would use a method that assesses the truthfulness of a victim's statement based on content criteria.
The more content criteria are present, the more truthful the statement is considered.
This is followed by four short clips (total of 2:49 minutes), one for each of the four CBCA criteria.

In these videos, the meaning of each criterion is explained and then demonstrated with two examples: one in which the criterion has a high presence and one in which the presence is low, to illustrate how different statements may look.

Subsequently, participants were presented with one of two counterbalanced practice statements, in which two of the criteria show high presence, and two show low presence (Practice Statement 1: CBCA criteria 1 and 3 are highly present, CBCA criteria 7 and 14 are weakly present; Practice Statement 2: CBCA criteria 1 and 3 are weakly present, CBCA criteria 7 and 14 are strongly present) Participants were then asked to rate the statement on all four criteria.
Afterwards, they received feedback regarding the expected rating and an explanation and answered four multiplechoice attention checks regarding the ranking of each criterion.
We used the credibility-reducing bias induction by Bogaard et al. (2014; see also Von Oppen et al 2026).

text.text: In essence, this contextual information provides a number of elements aimed to decrease the credibility of the victim.
We adapted the materials to our case and added additional elements to strengthen the bias.
We conducted a second pilot study (Pilot 2) and found moderate to strong reducing-credibility effects (see https://osf.io/afwc6/, shows the bias induction vs control context materials).

text.text: "This is a report of sexual abuse that allegedly took place several years ago.
Tina stated that her stepfather abused her.
The interrogation of Tina's mother showed that Tina has a lot of problems at school.
These problems are mainly due to her rebellious and deceitful behavior toward peers and teachers.
Tina also told the mother that she was raped by a friend six months ago but later admitted that this was consensual.
The relationship between the mother and Tina has recently deteriorated, partly because the victim has repeatedly stolen money.
The police officer interviewing Tina about the sexual abuse described her as very calm and without showing any signs of distress throughout several interviews.
The available security footage does not allow for verification of the timeline through confirmation of the suspect's and the victim's whereabouts within the house.
A befriended bartender reports that Stefan Kuhl was there watching a football game, and she remembers him staying after the game discussing why his team lost with other customers.
The suspect denies that the abuse has occurred.
The suspect also indicated that the alleged victim probably wants to get back at him, because he has denied Tina from going into the city with her friends, and this would be her way to do so.
The following statement was recorded in Düsseldorf, Germany, last autumn."
Victim Statement.
"Um, well, it was a normal school day.
My mother was out with a friend and he came home at seven or eight.
So he finished a bit later.
We said hello to each other as normal.
So I was lying in my bed, I was dressed in sweatpants and just a bra.
I'd already showered and everything, just ready for bed.
And I just wanted to eat dinner and then go to sleep. went to bed and then he came back and wanted to do it again.
But I was so wrapped up in my blanket that he couldn't do it again.
And then he just went out.
And then I slept, or rather, um, tried to sleep.
And then it was like that.
And then, um, it was school again the next day.
And then he asked me again the next day in the evening, so my mother was at sports and then he asked me if I wanted to do it again.
Um, and then I said no and then he let it go, um, and then he grabbed my ass or something when I bent over or something, for example, to get something out of a cupboard.
Or um, when I was eating, when my mother wasn't looking, he would stick his tongue out at me and then pretend he was licking a lollipop or something."

text.text: Pre-processing.
Participants who did not complete the study or who met the previously mentioned exclusion criteria (failed attention checks) were excluded from further analyses.
The CBCA score was calculated as the sum of the four criteria ratings.
The credibility score was based on the recorded rating.
We conducted an independent-sample t-test comparing the sequencing to the control condition on the CBCA sum score.
We used a two-tailed test because we did not expect a systematic difference in either direction.

Practice statement check: We ran four one-tailed independent Bayesian t-tests comparing Practice Statement 1 and 2 (independent variable) on the score for each CBCA criterion (score on CBCA criteria 1, 3, 7 or 14 as dependent variable).
We expected that participants who received Practice Statement 1 would score higher on criteria 1 and 3 than participants who received Practice Statement 2, as statements were designed as such.
In addition, we expected that participants with Practice Statement 2 would score higher on criteria 7 and 14 than participants with Practice Statement 1.
Therefore, the Bayesian t-tests compared models with a non-zero mean difference between practice statements to null models with equal means.
All Bayesian analyses were conducted in R using the BayesFactor package (Morey & Rouder, 2026).
text.formatted: All Bayesian analyses were conducted in R using the BayesFactor package <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Morey & Rouder, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: For Bayesian t-tests, ANOVAs, and linear regressions, we used the default Jeffreys-Zellner-Siow (JZS) priors with scale parameter r = 0.707 on standardized effect sizes, assuming normally distributed outcomes with equal variances across conditions.
Bayesian correlation analyses used the default Jeffreys-beta* prior on the correlation coefficient ρ and a normal likelihood.
Histograms and Q-Q plots of CBCA sum scores and credibility ratings indicated approximately normal distributions without severe deviations, supporting these modelling assumptions.
For key pairwise comparisons, we drew 10,000 posterior samples of the standardized effect size and report posterior means and 95% credible intervals (CrIs) where relevant.
We relied on these default priors and did not conduct additional formal sensitivity analyses of the Bayes factors to alternative prior specifications.

text.text: CBCA score.

The Bayesian one-way ANOVA investigating the effect of condition on the CBCA sum score revealed strong evidence for the model including condition compared to the intercept-only model (BFM = 18.40, see Table 3 for descriptive statistics).
text.formatted: The Bayesian one-way ANOVA investigating the effect of condition on the CBCA sum score revealed strong evidence for the model including condition compared to the intercept-only model (BFM = 18.40, see Table <ref type="table">3</ref> for descriptive statistics).

text.text: This is in line with our prediction and indicates a difference in CBCA sum scores across the three conditions.

A further Bayesian independent-samples t-test, investigating CBCA sum score across full information and control conditions, showed strong evidence that the CBCA sum scores were lower in the full information condition than in the control condition (BF10 = 40.22), and the posterior mean standardized effect size for this difference was d = 0.58 with a 95% CrI [0.21, 0.98], indicating that contextual bias was present in the CBCA sum score, which is in line with our prediction.

In addition, the Bayesian independent-samples t-test investigating CBCA sum score across full information and sequencing conditions yielded strong evidence for higher CBCA sum scores in the sequencing condition than in the full-information condition (BF10 = 13.15) and the posterior mean standardized effect size was d = 0.55 with a 95% CrI [-0.93,-0.17], indicating higher CBCA scores in the sequencing condition relative to the full-information condition.

Lastly, comparing the CBCA sum score across the sequencing condition and the control condition did not result in decisive evidence for either hypothesis but hints at there being no difference in CBCA between the control and sequencing condition (BF01 = 4.9).
The posterior mean standardized effect size was d < 0.00 with a 95% CrI [-0.35, 0.36], indicating that any difference between sequencing and control conditions in CBCA scores is likely to be small.

text.text: This is in line with our expectation, as both conditions did not receive the contextual bias information before the CBCA scoring.

The Bayesian one-way ANOVA investigating credibility differences across all three conditions yielded extreme evidence for the model including condition compared to an intercept-only model (BFM = 1883.68).
This is in line with our expectation and indicates that at least one pair of conditions differs.

Further, our planned contrasts comparing the credibility scores of the control and full-information conditions using Bayesian independent-samples t-tests yielded very strong evidence for higher credibility ratings in the control condition compared to the full-information condition (BF10 = 518.70).
The posterior mean standardized effect size was d = 0.75 with a 95% CrI [0.35, 1.15].

text.text: This is in line with our prediction and indicates that contextual bias was present in the credibility scores.
The Bayesian independent-samples t-tests comparing credibility scores of the full info and sequencing conditions showed a BF01 of 4.65.
The posterior mean standardized effect size was d = 0.06 with a 95% CrI [-0.29, 0.42].

This indicates that the observed data are about 4.65 times more likely under the model assuming no difference in credibility between the two conditions than under the model assuming a difference, which is consistent with the conclusion that sequencing does not protect against contextual bias in the credibility judgments.
To examine whether CBCA criteria scoring was correctly applied, we did four Bayesian independent-samples t-tests to compare how people rated the two practice statements.

Participants had been randomly assigned to a practice statement that was designed to score high on 2 and low on 2 other CBCA criteria (i.e., practice statement1 scored high on Logical Structure and Quantity of Details and low on Spontaneous Corrections and Unexpected Complications; practice statement1 scored high on Spontaneous Corrections and Unexpected Complications and low on Logical Structure and Quantity of Details).

As expected, there is extreme evidence that practice statement 1 was rated higher on logical structure (BF10 = 1.6 × 10²³) and quantity of detail (BF10 = 8.16 × 10⁷) compared to practice statement 2), whereas spontaneous corrections (BF10 = 7.62 × 10¹⁵) and unexpected complications (BF10 = 6.57 × 10⁹) were rated higher on statement 2.
These results indicate that participants were able to apply the criteria as intended for either practice statement.
Practice performance does not protect against contextual bias.
We were also interested in whether high practice statement performance would protect against bias in credibility judgments.
Therefore, we computed a practice proficiency index and computed a credibility bias score for the sequencing and the full information condition.

We then ran a Bayesian correlation analysis, which indicated that better practice performance did not systematically reduce or increase contextual bias in credibility (full information condition: r = 0.15, BF10 = 0.51; sequencing condition: r = 0.15, BF10 = 0.52); therefore, practice proficiency does not appear to protect against (or increase) contextual bias in credibility (see https://osf.io/afwc6/ for detailed analysis).

text.text: Ranking analysis.
As seen in Table 4, participants reported weighing logical structure and quantity of detail particularly in their final credibility assessment.
text.formatted: As seen in Table <ref type="table">4</ref>, participants reported weighing logical structure and quantity of detail particularly in their final credibility assessment.

text.text: This was confirmed by Bayesian linear models with final credibility judgement as the outcome and each CBCA criterion as a predictor and then compared each model to an intercept-only model.

The Single predictor models showed overwhelming evidence for quantity of detail (BF10 = 2.0 × 10 25 ) and logical structure (BF10 = 4.7 × 10 21 ) as predictors of credibility, moderate evidence for spontaneous corrections (BF10 ≈ 3.16), and evidence for the null model for unexpected complications (BF10 = 0.25) and the model including all four criteria provided extreme evidence over the intercept-only model (BF10 = 5.6 × 10 33 ).
As shown in Table 5, the mean CBCA scoring for each criterion was broadly consistent with participants' importance rankings and with their predictive value for credibility.
text.formatted: As shown in Table <ref type="table">5</ref>, the mean CBCA scoring for each criterion was broadly consistent with participants' importance rankings and with their predictive value for credibility.

text.text: We were also interested to see whether the association between CBCA scoring and credibility judgment differs by condition to see whether evaluators rely on CBCA to a different extent depending on the contextual information available in each condition.
Therefore, we performed Bayesian correlation analyses where models with a non-zero correlation between CBCA and credibility were compared to null models with ρ = 0 for each condition.

All three conditions yielded extreme evidence for a positive relationship between CBCA and credibility (control: BF10 = 4.6 × 10⁶, full information: BF10 = 6.9 × 10⁷, and sequencing: BF10 = 5.4 × 10⁶).
We followed it up with a Bayesian regression comparison between the main effect model (credibility ~ CBCA + condition) and interaction model (credibility ~ CBCA × condition).

It showed strong evidence against the interaction model (BF10 = 0.02), indicating a CBCA -credibility association of similar strength across conditions, rather than being moderated by condition (see Figure 2).

Credibility assessment of victim statements is a crucial source of evidence in sexual abuse cases (Volbert & Steller, 2014; De Jong & Rose, 1989).

text.text: A prominent tool to objectively assess credibility is the scoring of the statement content using the Criteria-Based Content Analysis (CBCA; Steller & Köhnken, 1989).
text.formatted: A prominent tool to objectively assess credibility is the scoring of the statement content using the Criteria-Based Content Analysis (CBCA; <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Steller & Köhnken, 1989)</ref>.

text.text: While CBCA scoring of the statements should be based on the content of the statement only, Bogaard et al. (2014) showed that extraneous information can influence the scoring.
text.formatted: While CBCA scoring of the statements should be based on the content of the statement only, <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Bogaard et al. (2014)</ref> showed that extraneous information can influence the scoring.

text.text: Here, we sought to examine the effectiveness of sequencing as a remedy to prevent extraneous information from influencing the CBCA-based content scoring of the statement.
Evidentiary independence is a crucial presumption in law, as the different pieces of evidence are interpreted as independent.
Yet, this does not seem to be the case; for example, it has been shown that knowing a suspect confessed can influence eyewitnesses' subsequent identification decisions (Hasel & Kassin, 2008).
text.formatted: Yet, this does not seem to be the case; for example, it has been shown that knowing a suspect confessed can influence eyewitnesses' subsequent identification decisions <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Hasel & Kassin, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, to assess all the different elements of evidence individually, we have to ensure that the assessment of each piece of evidence is not dependent on the others.
Multiple key findings result from the present study: We again found that the CBCA and the subsequent credibility assessment were both prone to contextual bias.
It follows that sequencing can prevent contextual bias in CBCA ratings, safeguarding the content scoring of the victim statement from extraneous influences.
Lastly, despite sequencing protecting CBCA scoring, contextual information still impacted the final credibility judgments.

The first key finding -that both CBCA scores and subsequent credibility assessments are vulnerable to contextual bias -highlights the susceptibility not only of the credibility judgment but also of the CBCA itself (Bogaard et al., 2014).
text.formatted: The first key finding -that both CBCA scores and subsequent credibility assessments are vulnerable to contextual bias -highlights the susceptibility not only of the credibility judgment but also of the CBCA itself <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bogaard et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: With this finding, we again replicate that contextual information -here knowing the victim's history of trouble at school, including rebellious and deceitful behavior toward peers, a prior rape accusation that was later recanted, a poor relationship with her mother, and repeated theft of money, as well as the accused's denial of the accusation by providing a motive for her to lie -changes the way people score the victim statement on specific content criteria.
This contextual information may have prompted prior assumptions or expectations that shaped how evaluators interpreted different aspects of the statement.
Because CBCA criteria are interpretive measures, they are sensitive to such influences.
The results indicate that evaluators' CBCA scores and credibility judgments are affected by what they already know about the case and the victim.

This pattern is consistent with prior work in forensic decision-making demonstrating that contextual information (e.g., suspect confessions, victim characteristics, or pre-existing theories) can contaminate expert judgments and now appears to extend to CBCA scores and credibility ratings, which are frequently used in legal and clinical practice (Dror et al., 2006; Hasel & Kassin, 2008; Ask & Granhag, 2005).
text.formatted: This pattern is consistent with prior work in forensic decision-making demonstrating that contextual information (e.g., suspect confessions, victim characteristics, or pre-existing theories) can contaminate expert judgments and now appears to extend to CBCA scores and credibility ratings, which are frequently used in legal and clinical practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Dror et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Hasel & Kassin, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Ask & Granhag, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: The shifts in judgment observed as a function of contextual information undermine their objectivity and underscore the need to interpret content scoring cautiously and to develop safeguards against contextual bias in credibility assessments.
The second key finding indicates that controlling the flow of information can mitigate contextual bias in CBCA ratings.
Evaluators who first assessed the victim's statement and only later received contextual information showed less bias in their CBCA scores compared to those exposed to contextual information earlier.
This suggests that the order in which information is presented shapes how strongly context can affect judgments.

This aligns with the linear sequential unmasking-expanded (LSU-E) approach, which proposes that experts should first examine the primary evidence in isolation and only then be exposed to case details to reduce confirmation bias (Dror & Kukucka, 2021; Dror et al., 2015).
text.formatted: This aligns with the linear sequential unmasking-expanded (LSU-E) approach, which proposes that experts should first examine the primary evidence in isolation and only then be exposed to case details to reduce confirmation bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Dror & Kukucka, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Dror et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Such sequencing is intended to preserve a more bottom-up analysis of the statement, as delaying contextual information may limit the formation of strong expectations and thereby reduce confirmation bias.
Indeed, the findings suggest that introducing sequencing as a tool to mitigate bias in credibility judgments can successfully protect the integrity of CBCA scores.

This supports the development of protocols in which independent assessors who are not involved in the interview process are initially "blinded" to potentially biasing contextual cues (e.g., prior allegations, suspect history, or victim history) until after the content-based assessment has been completed and documented, by structuring procedures so that CBCA evaluations are conducted before, and independent from, rich contextual case information.
The third key finding is that even when sequencing is used to protect CBCA ratings, contextual information continues to exert influence on final credibility judgments.
This suggests that structured sequencing can make the CBCA assessment more robust, yet it does not fully insulate the evaluators' final credibility judgment from bias once context is introduced.
Forming a credibility judgment is an integrative process that may be more vulnerable to contextual influences and intuitive, than rule-based scoring of individual criteria (Kahneman, 2011).
text.formatted: Forming a credibility judgment is an integrative process that may be more vulnerable to contextual influences and intuitive, than rule-based scoring of individual criteria <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Kahneman, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: The results, therefore, suggest that protecting the CBCA rating alone is not sufficient to protect the subsequent credibility judgment, as it remains vulnerable to contextual bias.
This highlights the need for further protective measures and safeguards at the level of the subsequent credibility judgment.

Additional protective measures could focus on ensuring that only relevant contextual factors, rather than irrelevant ones, influence the final judgment by structuring the subsequent credibility assessment more explicitly.
One approach would be to define and empirically test the factors that should be incorporated into the final credibility assessment within SVA (Volbert & Steller, 2014).
text.formatted: One approach would be to define and empirically test the factors that should be incorporated into the final credibility assessment within SVA <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Volbert & Steller, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: This could help ensure that final judgments are based on relevant information rather than on irrelevant contextual influences.
Choice of CBCA criteria.

When interpreting these findings, it is important to keep in mind that we used only four of the 19 CBCA criteria, and previous research has shown that the criteria differ in predictive power (Amado et al., 2016; Hauch et al., 2017; Arui et al., 2025).
text.formatted: When interpreting these findings, it is important to keep in mind that we used only four of the 19 CBCA criteria, and previous research has shown that the criteria differ in predictive power <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Amado et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Hauch et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Arui et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Future research should therefore examine sequencing on the full CBCA scale and test whether the observed debiasing pattern generalizes across different criterion sets.
Another important consideration is that real forensic interviews are typically interactive conversations rather than uninterrupted monologues. (Fernandes et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Another important consideration is that real forensic interviews are typically interactive conversations rather than uninterrupted monologues. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Fernandes et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In some cases, evaluators rely on written statements, but often on interviews that may vary considerably in structure and length.

In addition, it is important to note that our sample consisted of lay participants rather than experts, who completed only part of the SVA, i.e., not all required steps of the assessment were included in this study.
In this study, participants were not explicitly instructed to refrain from using background information in their credibility judgments.
They were asked to rate the statement and were reminded of the CBCA criteria.
Although they were neither encouraged nor instructed to use contextual information, it was not explicitly prohibited, so they may reasonably have treated it as evidence.
In German practice, additional information is considered before a final credibility judgment is made (Griesel et al., 2012).
text.formatted: In German practice, additional information is considered before a final credibility judgment is made <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Griesel et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: This begs the question of which information should be considered, and which should not.
Overall, this study shows that both CBCA ratings and global credibility judgments are vulnerable to contextual bias.
Sequencing case information can prevent bias in CBCA scores and make the credibility judgment process more transparent but does not equally protect the final credibility judgment.

Clearer guidelines on which contextual information may be relevant, together with procedures that promote transparency (e.g., two-stage judgments) in weighing in such contextual information may improve credibility assessments.

text.text: This raises a conceptual issue: are participants truly biased, or are they simply affected by contextual information that may be considered relevant?
Experts and lay people may differ in what is considered relevant (Griesel et al., 2012; Dror, 2017).
text.formatted: Experts and lay people may differ in what is considered relevant <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Griesel et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Dror, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: We have argued that we used contextual information that is objectively irrelevant for the task at hand -the content scoring of the statement.
This work should be expanded with research informing laypeople on what is (ir-)relevant and perhaps warning not to integrate contextual information.
The key issue likely is not whether contextual information should be used at all, but rather which pieces of information are reliable and relevant enough to weigh into the credibility assessment.

We think that an interesting avenue for future studies is to implement a two-stage judgment process where an independent evaluator gives judgments before and after contextual information is introduced (Dror & Kukucka, 2021; Kahneman et al., 2021).
text.formatted: We think that an interesting avenue for future studies is to implement a two-stage judgment process where an independent evaluator gives judgments before and after contextual information is introduced <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Dror & Kukucka, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Kahneman et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: First, the evaluator would provide CBCA ratings and then make an initial credibility judgment before any additional contextual information is introduced.
After this first credibility judgment, the contextual information would be presented, after which the same evaluator gives a second credibility judgment.
At this second stage, the evaluator would be required to explain whether and why they change their judgment.

Implementing such a procedure would make any changes in judgment more transparent to outside observers and could elicit more critical reflection, leading to more deliberate and well-justified credibility assessments than when no explanation is required (Maegherman et al., 2022).
